captions.instagram:
How does image recognition work?

To a computer, a mango is 2,304 numbers. Here a tiny camera renders one, hand-made filters find its edges, and a real neural network learns to tell mangoes from bananas, chillies and coins right in your browser. Then it finds them in a scene, draws boxes and masks, and gets fooled by invisible noise.

→ To a computer, a mango is not a mango. It is a grid of numbers.
→ Each pixel is three numbers: red, green and blue, from 0 to 255.
→ A CNN learns its own filters: edges first, then bigger parts, then an answer.
→ Show it 1,200 labelled pictures, again and again, and test it on new ones.
→ Slide the recogniser over the scene: every confident window becomes a box.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/visionclear (link in bio)

Box No. 078 of 365. Follow @glassbox.how for a new "how it works" every day.

youtubeLong.title: How does image recognition work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
To a computer, a mango is 2,304 numbers. Here a tiny camera renders one, hand-made filters find its edges, and a real neural network learns to tell mangoes from bananas, chillies and coins right in your browser. Then it finds them in a scene, draws boxes and masks, and gets fooled by invisible noise.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/visionclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/visionclear

In this video:
• A picture is only numbers. A camera sensor turns light into a grid of pixels, each with a red, green and blue value from 0 to 255.
• Filters find edges, layers find parts. A 3 × 3 grid of weights slid over the picture, a convolution, lights up where brightness jumps: edges.
• Learning from labelled pictures. A small CNN with 21,081 weights trains in your browser on 1,200 made-up pictures of a mango, banana, chilli, coin or nothing, and is tested on 300 wild ones it never saw.
• Where, not just what. Slide the recogniser over 897 windows of a scene and keep the confident ones.
• It fails in strange ways. A tiny change to every pixel, worked out from the network's own gradient, can flip its answer.
• Everywhere, with limits. Image recognition searches photos, helps screen for diabetic eye disease in India, suggests crop diseases, reads number plates and checks factory parts.

Glassbox opens one box a day: an interactive model of how something works, plus the code behind it.
